newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia seeks active OSCE role in local polls.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia seeks active OSCE role in local polls.

text.p: A Bosnian Moslem official criticised the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Wednesday for failing to take a more active role the country's election process.

The Moslem co-chairman of the country's goverment Haris Silajdzic told OSCE chairman, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, he was not satisfied with the OSCE's work in Bosnia and its mission head Robert Frowick.
Silajdzic demanded the OSCE take a more active role in ensuring conditions for free and democratic elections before the upcoming municipal elections set for September 13 and 14.
The OSCE is charged with supervising Bosnia's elections under the terms of the Dayton peace accord that ended a 43-month war in 1995.
Peterson called the criticism "unfair" and threw his support behind the mission and its chief Frowick.
"I have full confidence in the work of Ambassador (Robert) Frowick and the OSCE team here in doing their part of the job," Petersen told reporters.
"I think the parties themselves should ask themselves what they can do to secure the quality of elections, not merely ask the international community to provide the necessary conditions," he said.

The Dayton accord listed a number of conditions which must be met before voting can take place, including a politically neutral environment and freedom of movement, political association and expression.

The OSCE's previous chairman in office decided last year that Bosnia's general polls held in September 1996 were to go ahead despite the lack of conditions for free and fair elections throughout Bosnia, because a delay would have made the situation worse.
The country's local polls were not held with other polls in September last year and were postponed three times because of voter registration irregularities mainly by Serb and Croat nationalists.
Frowick said he had recommended local polls in September because further progress in preconditions had been made since last year.

The local polls are viewed as Bosnia's last chance for reunification because they should enable refugees to cross over to their former homes and cast votes, reversing the results of the war's ethnic cleansing.

Critics say conditions are by no means ripe: movement between Bosnia's Moslems, Croats and Serbs is very limited and many accuse the media of continuing to stir hatred, creating anything but a "politically neutral environment."
Local polls are expected only to confirm the nationalist parties' victories from last year's polls, they say.
